name: Cigarette butts

summary: The Cigarette butts calculator turns number of participants, the time cleaning and the containers filled into butts collected. It suits a footprint, a resource or an environmental change you want to size up. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Cigarette butts calculator work?
sections.html:
The Cigarette butts calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports butts collected in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (will you clean up only once or regularly?, the area and the I'll collect butts into (2)); then you type in number of participants, the time cleaning, how often will you clean up? and the containers filled.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• Will you clean up only once or regularly?: pick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as only once and regularly. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • Number of participants: a plain number with no unit attached.
  • Time cleaning: a measured quantity, entered by default in minutes. The unit chip switches it to any of the 27 supported units.
  • How often will you clean up?: a measured quantity, entered by default in weeks. The unit chip switches it to any of the 27 supported units.
  • Area: pick the option that matches your case — 4 options, such as dramatically polluted (beach, nightlife district), heavily polluted (city park, bus stop) and badly polluted (urban area). The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • I'll collect butts into (2): pick the option that matches your case — 8 options, such as 1L bottles/jars, 1.5L bottles and 2L bottles. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • Containers filled: a plain number with no unit attached.

3 fields on this form are a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Cigarette butts calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Butts collected=area × number of participants × time cleaning
Butts collected=170 × container volume × containers filled
Butts collected=area × how often will you clean up? × number of participants × time cleaning
Container volume=(1 ÷ 170) × butts collected ÷ containers filled
Container volume=I'll collect butts into...

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Butts collected: a number, filled in as soon as the inputs allow it.
  • Container volume: shown in liters, and convertible to any of the 40 units on that chip.
  • Butts collected (2): shown in years, and convertible to any of the 27 units on that chip.
  • Containers filled (2): shown in years, and convertible to any of the 27 units on that chip.
  • I'll collect butts into: a number, filled in as soon as the inputs allow it.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Time cleaning: Time, opening in minutes
  • How often will you clean up?: Time, opening in weeks
  • Container volume: Volume, opening in liters
  • Containers filled (2): Time, opening in years
  • Butts collected (2): Time, opening in years

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Cigarette butts calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Putting a headline figure into context
  • Comparing two options on the same basis
  • Sizing an environmental impact in familiar units
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — number of participants, the time cleaning and the containers filled — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Cigarette butts calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns butts collected, derived from number of participants, the time cleaning and the containers filled. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Cigarette butts calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for number of participants, the time cleaning and the containers filled, which is 7 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter time cleaning in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Time cleaning opens in minutes and the chip beside it offers 27 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (3 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports I'll collect butts into = 0. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Cigarette butts calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
